one_sentence: The Logos Thesis argues that information is the ontological primitive, from which General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics emerge as limit cases of a single coherence scale, and that the closing structure requires a Trinitarian operator set.
executive_summary: The Logos Thesis addresses the century-long incompatibility between General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics by identifying it as an ontological crisis rooted in Material Primacy. It introduces the Logos Field (χ) as a non-material, self-grounding informational substrate that resolves three foundational failures: the Compression Crisis (algorithmic efficiency), the Measurement Boundary (von Neumann's infinite regress), and the Consciousness Integration Problem (substrate-independent agency). The framework derives a Master Equation showing GR and QM as high- and low-coherence limits of a single coherence scale. It further demonstrates that Moral Entropy (Law V) exhibits irreversibility, requiring the non-unitary work input of an external operator (Ĝ). Through formal constraint elimination, the thesis concludes that the minimal operator structure satisfying all physical and functional boundary conditions is Triadic Closure—three non-commutative operators mapping to the Trinitarian ontology. The framework is empirically testable via a Pre-Registered Falsification Protocol with explicit kill-criteria.
short_summary: This document is a formal thesis proposing the Logos Field (χ) as a non-material informational substrate that resolves the incompatibility between General Relativity and Quantum Mechanics. The core structural claim is that GR and QM emerge as high- and low-coherence limits of a single coherence scale governed by the χ-field. Key evidence includes the resolution of the Compression Crisis, Measurement Boundary, and Consciousness Integration Problem, along with a derived Master Equation and a Pre-Registered Falsification Protocol. This matters because it offers a unified, empirically testable framework that identifies the Trinitarian structure as a physical necessity, not a theological assumption.
